title: A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory that predicts how well a learning system will perform on previously unseen data from its architecture, training data and training procedure, before the training run takes place. It would explain why systems that can memorize their training examples sometimes learn patterns that transfer to new examples. Its predictions would need to be informative enough to guide practical decisions, with explicit assumptions and uncertainty, rather than bounds so loose that they accommodate both useful and effectively random performance.

Proposed scope: the ambition is to cover practically trained modern systems, including transformers and generative models. Predicting failures under specified changes in the data distribution is an additional target beyond predicting performance on new examples drawn from the training distribution. These are intended capabilities of the innovation, not coverage requirements established by the supplied surveys. A successful theory could have several explicitly bounded regimes; it need not promise prediction for every possible architecture, task or distribution shift.

significance.text: The scientific motivation is a gap between successful practice and available explanations. Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht and Vinyals showed that image-classification networks capable of learning real labels could also fit randomly assigned labels. This challenges explanations that rely only on the model's capacity to fit data and its explicit regularization: those features alone do not adequately distinguish useful learning from memorization in the tested settings. The result does not invalidate all complexity-based theories, implicit regularization or classical statistical learning theory. Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin describe substantial theoretical progress alongside persistent explanatory gaps.

Impact synthesis: if the proposed theory made accurate prospective predictions across practically important regimes, it could play a role analogous to a constitutive law for an engineering material. Designers could use a validated relationship between training choices and expected performance to compare candidate systems before committing to expensive runs. The analogy has limits: the predictions would hold within the theory's assumptions, and average predictive accuracy would not automatically establish a guarantee for every trained model or deployment circumstance.

Conditional downstream possibilities include more principled architecture selection, training allocation and data collection. Calculating data requirements would require validated predictions across sample sizes, rather than one successful prediction at one dataset size. Anticipating failures under distribution shift would require assumptions describing the shifts covered by the theory. More capable agents and more dependable physical autonomy could benefit from these advances, but neither follows from a theory of generalization alone.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is a quantitatively useful connection between the specification of a practical training process and its resulting generalization. The 2021 survey presents implicit regularization and benign overfitting in simpler settings as examples illuminating broader conjectured principles. The challenge is to retain that explanatory power when moving beyond tractable models and limiting regimes to the systems actually trained. A theory must distinguish conditions under which fitting training data supports useful prediction from conditions under which it primarily supports memorization.

Uniform-convergence analyses, neural-tangent models and mean-field limits provide different kinds of insight under restricted assumptions. They should not be treated as interchangeable explanations or as a completed account of realistic deep learning. The reviewed portions of Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin discuss linearized neural-tangent behavior and a contrasting mean-field regime, while emphasizing the need to extend understanding beyond linear models. The scientific and engineering barrier is to identify when such approximations describe practical training accurately enough to support useful numerical predictions, and how to proceed when they do not.

Generative modeling introduces an additional problem: the quantity a theory predicts must meaningfully reflect the behavior people want from the model. Marion and Wu's diffusion-model position paper argues that test loss can reveal memorization while correlating poorly with visual quality. Consequently, a prediction of held-out loss alone would not establish a theory of useful generation. A broader account would need to connect training to suitable measures of fidelity and novelty, while making clear which aspects of generative behavior those measures capture.

Proposed engineering requirements: prospective prediction also requires a sufficiently precise training specification, an evaluation metric, an uncertainty interpretation and a defined domain of applicability. For distribution-shift predictions, the shifts themselves must be specified. Otherwise, a failure could reflect an unspecified change in the problem rather than a discriminating test of the theory. These requirements define a useful research target; the supplied evidence does not establish a general solution to them.

current_state.text: Zhang and colleagues' paper was first submitted in November 2016 and published at ICLR 2017. Its random-label experiments demonstrated that successful image-classification networks could fit labels that carried no meaningful relationship to the images. The paper also concluded that explicit regularization can improve generalization but is neither necessary nor sufficient by itself to control generalization error. These experiments motivate the theoretical problem; they do not show that generalization is inexplicable or that every existing theoretical approach fails. The supplied review reports a complete retained text, including appendices, and its assessment did not depend on visual inspection of figures.

Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin's 2021 Acta Numerica survey organizes theoretical progress on implicit regularization and benign overfitting, including quadratic-loss regression and linearized networks. It presents simpler settings that illustrate conjectured principles and discusses neural-tangent and mean-field regimes. This is evidence of substantial partial understanding, alongside challenges in extending it to realistic deep learning. The supplied review had access to the abstract and a PDF extraction ending during page 38; its conclusions about the inspected passages are supported, but the extraction does not permit assessment of all later discussion.

The supplied bibliography lists Suh and Cheng's A Survey on Statistical Theory of Deep Learning: Approximation, Training Dynamics, and Generative Models as first published on November 21, 2024, with a 2025 volume citation of volume 12, pages 177–207. However, the source index contains no retained document or abstract for this entry. Its coverage, document identity and volume details therefore cannot be confirmed from source content in the supplied review. The earlier research's descriptions of its abstract, including what it does or does not claim about frontier language models, cannot serve as verified evidence here.

Pierre Marion and Yu-Han Wu's May 2026 arXiv version 1 position paper argues that understanding diffusion-model generalization requires frameworks beyond classical statistical learning theory and supervised benign overfitting. Its discussion of the mismatch between test loss and generative quality sharpens the evaluation problem. This is an attributed argument in a preprint, not a consensus theorem or a demonstration that all alternative frameworks fail. The supplied review reports complete retained text through references and appendices; figures were not visually inspected, so the assessment rests on the authors' textual statements.

Evidence synthesis as of November 1, 2026: the reviewed material documents historical experiments, restricted theoretical successes and an argument for further conceptual work. It does not establish a theory meeting the proposed breadth and predictive requirements. The supplied bounded search record is empty, however, so it also cannot establish that no such theory existed by that date. The innovation remains a proposed capability in this record; the incomplete evidence base establishes neither achievement nor exhaustive absence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: preregister a theory-derived prediction before training a new transformer or diffusion model on a dataset not used to tune the theory. Fix the training specification, evaluation metric, tolerance and interpretation of uncertainty in advance. Compare the result with the prediction and with a stated random baseline appropriate to the task. A bound too loose to distinguish useful performance from that baseline would not meet this proposed criterion. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered untuned-data prediction separates useful performance from random baseline

completion_criteria.text: For a diffusion-model demonstration, include evaluation that captures fidelity and novelty rather than relying only on held-out training loss. The reason is substantive: the reviewed position paper describes test loss as informative about memorization but poorly aligned with visual quality. The protocol would need to state what each selected measure demonstrates and what behavior it leaves untested.
completion_criteria.label: Diffusion fidelity and novelty measures state tested and untested behavior

completion_criteria.text: Proposed broader validation: repeat prospective tests across independent datasets, training runs, model sizes and the architecture families claimed to fall within the theory. If data-requirement prediction is claimed, test across sample sizes; if distribution-shift prediction is claimed, test explicitly defined shifts. Independent teams should be able to reproduce the predictions and evaluations using documented assumptions and procedures. A single successful run would establish an initial example, while finite repeated tests would establish demonstrated breadth rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective tests repeated across the claimed scope are independently reproducible

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report where predictions are informative, where uncertainty becomes too large to guide a decision, and how much computation or data is required to produce the prediction. Include a testable limitation or contrasting regime that probes the theory's applicability. Do not require predictions to fail whenever sufficient hypotheses are violated: a conclusion can remain true outside the conditions that guarantee it. Strong evidence would combine useful prospective accuracy with a clear account of assumptions, exceptions and remaining uncertainty.
completion_criteria.label: Report decision-guiding range, resource costs, and a testable limitation

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models, is the closest adjacent entry. CSC-06 concerns predicting generalization from architecture, data and training; CSC-10's title concerns machine-checked guarantees about model behavior. A generalization theory might supply assumptions or results useful to a guarantee, and verification might formalize parts of the theory. Nevertheless, a prospective error estimate does not automatically constitute a checked behavioral guarantee, and a guarantee for a particular model does not automatically provide a predictive theory across training specifications. Only CSC-10's title is supplied, so its detailed scope remains unspecified.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-03, Competent general machine intelligence, and CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments, concern broader capabilities. Predictive generalization theory could help developers anticipate performance and identify specified transfer failures relevant to both. It would not itself demonstrate general intelligence or reliable physical action, whose requirements extend beyond predicting a learning system's error.

Roster-based synthesis: CSC-07, Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery, could overlap through the discovery or verification of generalization theorems. CSC-04, Industrial-cost proof-carrying software, shares an interest in formal reasoning that can support practical engineering. These remain distinct goals: producing or checking proofs does not by itself establish that a theorem's assumptions adequately describe practical learning, and predicting statistical performance does not by itself produce proof-carrying software.

brief.title: Predicting how well AI will learn before training
possible: People building AI could compare designs before paying for expensive training runs. A theory would predict performance on unfamiliar examples from the model’s design, training data and training procedure. It would explain when learning transfers to new examples and when a model merely memorizes.

The goal includes transformers, a type of model design, and diffusion models, which learn to remove noise to generate data. Predictions could also cover failures when incoming data changes in specified ways.
why: AI developers could make more informed choices about model design, computing budgets and data collection. Predicting how performance changes with the amount of training data could help them work out how much data they need.

The scientific puzzle is that models able to memorize meaningless examples can also learn useful patterns. Explaining that difference would connect successful practice to a theory that guides engineering decisions.

sources.who: Chiyuan Zhang, Samy Bengio, Moritz Hardt, Benjamin Recht and Oriol Vinyals
sources.showed: Image classifiers that learned meaningful labels could also memorize randomly assigned labels. Their ability to fit examples did not distinguish useful learning from memorization.
sources.quote: Deep neural networks easily ﬁt random labels.
sources.cited_for: The central puzzle: the same model can learn useful patterns or memorize meaningless labels.
sources.not_established: These experiments do not provide a theory that predicts performance before training.

sources.who: Peter L. Bartlett, Andrea Montanari and Alexander Rakhlin
sources.showed: They surveyed explanations of why fitting training data very closely can coexist with accurate predictions. Mathematical results cover simpler models and restricted conditions.
sources.quote:
For these methods, we can decompose the prediction rule into a
simple component that is useful for prediction and a spiky component that is useful for overﬁtting but,
in a favorable setting, does not harm prediction accuracy.
sources.cited_for: There is substantial partial understanding of why memorization need not spoil predictions.
sources.not_established: Results in simpler settings do not establish useful predictions for practical modern systems.

sources.showed: This is a survey of statistical theory covering deep learning, training dynamics and generative models.
sources.cited_for: It provides background on statistical theories of deep learning.
sources.not_established: A survey alone does not demonstrate accurate predictions before practical training runs.

sources.showed: Their preprint combines a position paper with image-generation experiments. They report a mismatch between prediction error on withheld examples and generated image quality.
sources.quote: neural networks used in standard pipelines do have the capacity to memorize the training data.
sources.cited_for: Evaluating generation requires measures of both quality and freedom from copying.
sources.not_established: Their experiments do not establish that the findings extend to larger models and datasets.

shown: Zhang and colleagues demonstrated that successful image classifiers could also memorize random labels. Bartlett, Montanari and Rakhlin surveyed mathematical explanations of useful prediction despite closely fitting training data, chiefly in simpler settings.

Marion and Wu argue in a preprint that diffusion models need explanations tied to what they generate. Their experiments sharpen the evaluation problem, but do not establish a broadly predictive theory.
missing: Useful numerical predictions from practical training specifications, accurate enough to distinguish learning from chance.
Demonstrations that simplified mathematical models describe practical training closely enough to guide decisions.
Predictions of generated quality and novelty, meaning freedom from copying training examples.
Repeated independent tests with explicit assumptions, uncertainty and defined changes in incoming data.

milestones.label: An advance prediction distinguishes useful learning from chance
milestones.explanation: A prediction registered before training a new transformer or diffusion model on data unused to tune the theory would have to pass fixed evaluation rules. It must distinguish useful performance from chance.

milestones.label: Generation measures capture quality and freedom from copying
milestones.explanation: A diffusion-model test would have to measure quality and novelty, stating what each measure tests and leaves untested. Prediction error alone does not establish useful generation.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce predictions across the claimed scope
milestones.explanation: Advance predictions would have to hold across datasets, runs, model sizes and claimed designs, including data amounts or defined data changes where claimed. Independent reproduction would establish demonstrated breadth.

milestones.label: Useful range, prediction costs and a limitation are explicit
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish where predictions guide decisions, where uncertainty becomes too large, their computing and data costs, and a testable limitation. This would define practical use and boundaries.

uncertain: Which model designs and changes in incoming data should fall within the theory’s scope?
How accurate and inexpensive must predictions be to guide practical decisions?
Which measures adequately capture generated quality and novelty, and which chance comparisons suit each task?

page.title: A predictive theory of deep learning generalization
page.definition: A mathematical theory predicts performance on new examples drawn from a specified distribution before a neural network is trained, from its architecture, training data and training procedure. Its assumptions and prediction errors are explicit, and its predictions distinguish learning from memorization within a stated domain.

goal.need: ImageNet experiments separate memorization from transfer: the same architecture fits real and randomized labels, with different held-out accuracy. Predicting that difference could inform training choices. OpenAI reports predicting GPT-4’s held-out code loss from runs using at most 1/10,000 of its compute. The prediction used a scaling law fitted to smaller runs.

figures.caption: Inception v3 accuracy on ImageNet, reported on 26 February 2017.
figures.note: 1,281,167 training images; 50,000 validation images; 1,000 classes. Data augmentation, dropout and weight decay were disabled. Values are top-1 accuracy.

statements.body: National Science Foundation, Mathematical Foundations of Artificial Intelligence solicitation
statements.quote: rigorous approaches for characterizing and validating machine learning algorithms and their predictions
A large focus of the GPT-4 project was building a deep learning stack that scales predictably.

statements.body: NeurIPS 2020 Predicting Generalization in Deep Learning competition organisers
statements.quote: design metrics that accurately predict the generalization performance of deep neural networks without using a test set.
statements.context: The competition takes trained networks and their training data as inputs.

completion.title: Independent experiments confirm a theory’s numerical predictions made before training.
completion.criterion: An independent group validates a published mathematical theory’s predictions of performance on a specified unseen-data distribution for finite neural networks, from architecture, training data and training procedure. Predictions are fixed before target training begins and meet error tolerances fixed before outcomes are observed, across the theory’s stated range of datasets, sample sizes and training choices. They distinguish useful performance from a stated baseline. Assumptions and uncertainty are explicit; prediction parameters are not fitted to validation outcomes. Generative or distribution-shift claims require corresponding metrics or specified shifts.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external completion test for this combined capability was located.
completion.basis: Searched NSF foundations solicitations, DARPA AIQ requirements, NeurIPS PGDL rules and generalization surveys for a pretraining prediction standard; none supplied a completion test or common accuracy tolerance. The 2021 survey establishes results in restricted regimes. AIQ’s 5% target permits evaluation results as inputs. The learning-mechanics preprint calls for first-principles predictions; diffusion work questions test loss as a generation metric. This fallback requires independent prospective validation within a declared domain.

milestones.title: An overparameterized neural classifier receives a proved error bound below 100%.
milestones.criterion: For a neural classifier with more parameters than training examples, prove an upper bound below 1 on expected error on new examples, with sampling assumptions and confidence specified. This is nonvacuity, not accurate error prediction. Dziugaite and Roy’s 2017 binary-MNIST experiment used 55,000 training and 10,000 test images. For approximately 2.384 million parameters, the stochastic-classifier bound was 0.223 at confidence 0.965; its test-error upper estimate was 0.035. The bound was computed after training.
milestones.set_by: Statistical-learning convention of a nonvacuous classification-risk bound, stated by Dziugaite and Roy in UAI 2017.
milestones.threshold_quote: before the generalization error falls below 1.

milestones.title: A generalization predictor ranks first on the PGDL competition’s four final tasks.
milestones.criterion: Achieve the highest final-phase score under the NeurIPS 2020 PGDL protocol, predicting relative generalization from trained networks and training data without test-set access. The conditional-mutual-information score measures information about pairwise performance rankings after conditioning on training settings, averaged across four hidden image-classification tasks. Interpex ranked first with 22.92 points out of 100 among 24 final-phase teams. The complete benchmark contained 454 networks across eight tasks. This tests ranking after training.
milestones.set_by: NeurIPS 2020 PGDL organisers, final-phase competition scoring and winner selection; the benchmark covers convolutional image classifiers.
milestones.threshold_quote: the highest scoring solution is used for determining the final winners.

milestones.title: An AIQ method predicts an unevaluated test value within 5% of that value.
milestones.criterion: Meet DARPA AIQ’s specific-problem target: predict test values from training data and evaluation results within 5% of the test value. The programme requires results for more than one model and evaluation on Llama plus another listed model family. This permits measurements of trained models. On 5 October 2026, Kitware reported evaluating a method across approximately 100 models and benchmarks, but published no prediction-error values establishing the 5% target. That account is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: DARPA AIQ, BAA HR001124S0029, Amendment 04, Section I, specific-problem evaluation; DARPA’s document text is reproduced by GovTribe.
milestones.threshold_quote: predictions should be within 5% of the test value.

milestones.title: A theory’s predictions made before training agree with experiments within its stated error tolerance.
milestones.criterion: The theory’s developers obtain numerical agreement on new training runs within tolerances fixed in advance, using architecture, training data and training procedure without target-run outcomes. The demonstration covers the theory’s declared domain; independent confirmation remains the completion test. GPT-4’s reported code-loss extrapolation used no partial target-run results, but was fitted to smaller runs and made after target training began. Its report does not establish this pretraining test.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; no externally specified stage testing theory-derived numerical predictions fixed before target training begins was found in NSF, AIQ or PGDL requirements.

not_found: No external completion criterion or accuracy tolerance for generalization predictions made before training was found.
No external protocol defining the prospective-validation milestone was found.
